1.0.0.en: The Apostle James opens his epistle with the words “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus” to show the divinity of the Lord Christ. Although he was called the brother of the Lord, he remained humble and called himself a servant of Jesus Christ. Just as a servant has no authority over his own body, his wife or his children, so the Apostle James says that he is a “servant” with joy, because he has surrendered his whole life and his possessions to the Lord, as the Virgin Mary said, “Behold the handmaid of the Lord.” Her joy that she would be the mother of God the Word incarnate did not make her forget that she was a handmaid of God.

1.0.1.en: The Dispersion: the Christians of Jewish origin were scattered throughout the world after the martyrdom of Stephen because of persecution, so the Apostle James wrote them this epistle to strengthen and encourage them and to reinforce their faith. He also wrote to all believers who were persecuted and to all the Jews who had believed and who had formerly lived among the Gentiles.

1.0.2.en: May we not forget that we are servants of God, and may we surrender our whole life to Him, however much boldness of sonship we have.

1.0.3.en: (2) How do we endure trials? (vv. 2-12:) 2 “My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations; 3 Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience. 4 But let patience have her perfect work, that ye may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing. 5 If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him. 6 But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed. 7 For let not that man think that he shall receive any thing of the Lord. 8 A double minded man is unstable in all his ways. 9 Let the brother of low degree rejoice in that he is exalted: 10 But the rich, in that he is made low: because as the flower of the grass he shall pass away. 11 For the sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass, and the flower thereof falleth, and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth: so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways. 12 Blessed is the man that endureth temptation: for when he is tried, he shall receive the crown of life, which the Lord hath promised to them that love him.”

1.1.1.en: All joy: trials bring many blessings that gladden the soul.

1.1.2.en: Fall: this means that trials come upon the believer from outside, but without the person falling into sin. This kind of trial is to prove the person, as God tested Abraham. God gives the trial according to what a person can bear, but if the person sins during the trial, as Job murmured, God supports him until he repents, and in this way he also benefits from the trial.

1.1.3.en: When God allows trials to come upon us, we are not troubled, but we trust in the many blessings we shall receive from them, and our hearts rejoice. The following verses show the blessings of trials, which are:

1.2.1.en: The first means of enduring a trial and succeeding in it is to be patient in it, because pain is hard for a person, but by being patient in it we receive blessings.

1.3.1.en: The second means is to accompany patience with spiritual works such as prayer, fasting, prostrations (metanoias) and thanksgiving, and to continue in these works, striving toward Christian perfection. Thus we grow spiritually in our relationship with God.

1.4.1.en: A trial creates problems, so a person is perplexed about how to act and needs wisdom to act well and pass through the trial. The Apostle offers a simple solution, which is to ask for it from God in faith, and He will surely give. His giving is marked by two things:

1.4.2.en: a- Abundantly and generously, more than we ask.

1.4.3.en: b- With fatherly love, so He does not upbraid us for our weakness and ignorance, but on the contrary covers us and honors us.

1.5.1.en: God is ready to give us wisdom, but on condition of faith, and that we be ready to do what He asks of us and trust that the trial is for our good. As for the one who wavers, that is, the doubter, he is like a wave of the sea, which rises and rushes to the shore and then draws back. Such a person lives anxious and disturbed, unable to make the right decision. For the mind of the one who wavers is not convinced that God’s way is the best, and such a one must be sure that he will not receive anything from the Lord, because he does not believe in God’s wisdom and power.

1.5.2.en: A double minded man: a person who wavers between relying on God and depending on his own mind, his abilities and the powers of the world; or who wavers between holding to God’s commandments and using the evil means of the world, so that he uses one course at times and then the other. Such a person will suffer disturbance and instability in all the affairs of his life.

1.6.1.en: The spiritual person, facing a trial, remembers his sins, repents and prays with lowliness before God, and when he humbles himself in this way, God removes from him the feelings of distress and comforts his heart, so his spirit is lifted up and he blesses God and thanks Him. This is the rejoicing in God’s raising him up, that is, thanksgiving.

1.7.0.en: 6- Being a stranger to the world:

1.7.1.en: The one who feels that he is a stranger to the world and that it passes away can accept the trial and the loss of material things, because in his sight they are transient. The Apostle likens them to flowers that quickly fall to the ground and wither. Therefore it is fitting for the rich, and likewise for each one of us, to feel that everything we own is transient, so that if trials take it away we are not troubled, and we trust that the true wealth is in life with God and the Kingdom of Heaven. But whoever depends on material things will wither like them, that is, he will not enjoy true happiness with God on earth and will receive nothing in heaven.

1.8.0.en: The Apostle concludes his words about enduring trial by giving good news to the one who endures it, following the means mentioned before in the previous verses and passing through the trial successfully: he receives the heavenly crown in the Kingdom, that is, enjoyment with God forever.

1.8.1.en: Do not be troubled by the trials that pass over you. However hard they seem, trust that God’s help will not leave you, and that God allowed them so that you may advance in your spiritual life and be delivered by them from every evil.

1.9.s.en: (3) Inward temptations and the goodness of God

1.9.0.en: When he is tempted: he fell into sin because of the temptation.

1.9.1.en: He moves on to another kind of temptation, the inward temptations, that is, the heart’s responding to evil and falling into sin. If this happens, a person must not think that God is the One who created in him a nature inclined to evil or pushed him into evil by this temptation. Why? Because God is righteous, holy and perfect, so no one can tempt Him, in the sense of making Him fall into sin. And so, because He is luminous, He does not by nature incline toward darkness or toward making people fall into it, in the sense of tempting them in order to make them fall.

1.9.2.en: As for the former trials, which are a divine testing, they mean God’s attempt to raise a person to higher degrees in order to reward him with a greater reward.

1.10.0.en: The true cause of falling into temptation is the stirring of lust in a person’s heart and his being deceived by the devil’s wiles, so that he is drawn to the outward pleasure of sin and falls into its evil and bitterness.

1.11.0.en: He makes clear the seriousness of inward response and of falling into temptation. A person is drawn to the pleasure of sin by his evil carnal inclinations, and this he likens to conception. Lust makes a person fall into actual sin, and he likens sin to the child born of the conception. Then the penalty of sin is death and eternal torment. So if a person continues in his sins all his life, his sin is completed and he is condemned to eternal death. This is like a person who desires to possess, so he falls into the sin of theft and is then sentenced to prison; this is a temptation to which a person responded inwardly with evil feelings. The opposite is Joseph the righteous, who endured slavery in the house of Potiphar and then the sufferings of prison, and received God’s reward, which was the throne of Egypt. This was an outward trial to prove Joseph and reward him.

1.11.1.en: Driving out evil thoughts saves you from many sins. Satan breaks up your strength and weakens you with a multitude of thoughts, so that when he presents actual sin to you afterward, your fall is easy. So guard against thoughts, sights and words, lest you fall into hard temptations that destroy your life.

1.12.0.en: The Apostle forbids us to accuse God of being the cause of our sins and problems. The cause of our sins, as he mentioned, is our being drawn by our lusts toward evil, but God is good and the source of all blessings.

1.13.0.en: Father of lights: the source of all light and good on earth.

1.13.1.en: With whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning: the planets revolve and their position changes, and from this results the change of climate in the seasons of the year and the succession of night and day; and in ancient times time was known by the shadow. But God has nothing of this, because He is constant and perfect.

1.13.2.en: The Apostle declares that the source of all the good gifts we enjoy, and of all the talents and abilities we have, is God, the Giver of blessings, and that He is constant and continuous in His giving, not like changeable human beings, who, however good they seem, change and die.

1.14.1.en: A kind of firstfruits of his creatures: in ancient times the Jews offered the firstfruits of their crops and their animals to God, and these were holy and distinct from the rest because they belonged to God. So believers are the firstfruits of the world, so that many others may believe, and because of them God blesses the whole earth with the animals and plants in it.

1.14.2.en: The greatest grace we have received is the new birth through Baptism, so we became children of Christ the Savior and the beginning of the Church, which will include the many who will believe throughout the ages.

1.15.s.en: (4) The conduct of the children of God

1.15.0.en: The Apostle draws the believer’s attention to some important virtues in his life, namely that he be:

1.15.1.en: 1- Swift to hear: the person who listens well understands more and finds an opportunity to ask God to guide him in what he will say; he is also restful to others and establishes a stronger relationship of love with them, and the result is that he is slow to speak, that is, not impulsive. As Solomon the Wise says, “Seest thou a man that is hasty in his words? there is more hope of a fool than of him” (Prov 29:20). So then, should we be silent or speak? The saints say, “Speaking for God’s sake is good, and silence for God’s sake is good also.”

1.15.2.en: 2- Slow to wrath: the true Christian does not become angry with others, but is like his heavenly Father, who is longsuffering, “for the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God.”

1.15.3.en: But the acceptable anger is a person’s anger at himself, that is, repentance, and it is also called holy anger.

1.15.4.en: 3- Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness: when a person calms down in his speech with others, he must attend to repentance and the rejection of every kind of filthiness, whether evil thoughts, bad sights, foul speech, all acts of fornication, and the many evils connected with them.

1.15.5.en: 4- Receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls: repentance gives a person purity, so he receives the word of God that he reads in the Holy Bible or hears in the Church and submits to it with humility and calm, and the word is implanted in his heart, affects him and leads him in the way of salvation. This shows the importance of reading the word of God and attending spiritual meetings.

1.16.0.en: 5- Doers of the word: because whoever hears and does not do deceives himself that he is religious and knows much, but the measure is not knowledge but carrying out the commandment in practice.

1.17.0.en: The Apostle likens the one who hears the word and does not do it to a man who looks in a mirror and does not correct his appearance, but goes away and forgets his defects. The believer, however, must look attentively into the word of God, which is a mirror that reveals to him his weakness, his faults and his shortcomings, and so he receives it with meekness and corrects himself, striving toward holiness, truth and perfection, so as to be like his heavenly Father and to keep the image he received by the new birth.

1.18.0.en: If the Law of Moses was commands in the letter, with ordinances and judgments that a person carried out as a slave, as a duty and an obligation, and then forgot them, the law of Christ is otherwise, for it is the law of the freedom of the children of God, out of love. It is called the perfect law because it brings a person to perfection by grace and the work of the Holy Spirit. And whoever abides in the word of God, applying it in his life, his works are blessed by God and he enjoys joy and peace.

1.19.0.en: 6- Bridling his tongue: whoever believes himself to be holy and religious but does not control his tongue deludes himself with a false piety and deceives himself that he knows God when he does not know Him, because he rages, becomes angry, curses and judges others, and thinks that he has become a reformer of them.

1.20.0.en: 7- Mercy: the Apostle James sums up the concept of pure religion as:

1.20.1.en: 1- Works of compassion joined to faith, and mercy toward orphans and widows who have no one to provide for them.

1.20.2.en: 2- A person’s keeping his heart in purity and holiness and the cleanness of thought, and putting the word of God into practice in his life with patience, love and joy.

1.20.3.en: Therefore the believer should keep away from every source of pollution of hearing and sight, so that he may be sanctified to God in body, soul and spirit.

1.20.4.en: Offer your love to all around you and have compassion on everyone, for there is no person who is not exposed to troubles. Care especially for those whom others do not care for, or who suffer from a sense of loneliness, and trust that this work of mercy fills your heart with peace, pours God’s mercies upon you, and gladdens your heart when you see the smile on the faces of those to whom you showed mercy.

2.0.0.en: Baptism gives believers a new birth, so that they all become brothers without distinction, bias or preferring one believer over another, but all are members of the one Body of Christ. True faith is bound to love for all without distinction, because Christ, the Lord of glory, will show partiality to no one in heaven but will glorify all with Him, each one according to his works, without regard to his position or wealth or any worldly abilities he has.

2.1.0.en: Your assembly: he did not say “your church”, because partiality does not befit the Church, and by it she becomes like a Jewish synagogue.

2.1.1.en: He rebukes their partiality to the rich man, whom he describes as having splendid clothes and gold rings, so they give him a great place to sit in. But the poor man, whose clothes are shabby and dirty, they do not give the right to sit beside the rich man, but he stands far off or sits on the ground. The seriousness of the sin of partiality appears in two matters:

2.1.2.en: 1- Partiality is far from faith, since it considers that the rich are the pillar of the Church and not God who gave them wealth.

2.1.3.en: 2- Partiality is an insult to the poor person, who is created in the image of God, and it is an insult to Christ Himself, who became poor to enrich us, as they said of Him, “Is not this the carpenter’s son?”

2.1.4.en: Moreover, by it we belittle brothers of ours in the faith, who are members of the one Body of Christ.

2.2.0.en: Are ye not then partial in yourselves: partiality is far from the fear of God. So you who show partiality, will you not review yourself and doubt this conduct of yours, so as to repent of it?

2.2.1.en: Partiality springs from evil thoughts, so he asks them to judge their consciences, that is, to be judges of their evil thoughts, review them and repent of them.

2.3.0.en: The Apostle shows that material wealth does not matter to God, and that many of the saints were poor, such as Moses the shepherd, whom God called from the bush, and David the shepherd, whom God anointed king, and likewise most of the disciples of Christ were fishermen and poor people. These became heirs of the heavenly Kingdom that He prepared for them. He shows the importance of spiritual wealth through faith on earth and the inheritance of the Kingdom, and this is better than all material wealth.

2.3.1.en: This does not mean that wealth is evil, but the evil is that a person forgets God because of his preoccupation with wealth and falls into pride.

2.4.0.en: The believers in the Church were influenced by wealth, so they honored the rich and despised the poor, and forgot that wicked rich people use their money and influence to insult the believers and stir up the wicked against them (Acts 19:25-29), and likewise to bring them to trial and throw them into prisons.

2.5.0.en: The rich go on in their evil and blaspheme the name of Christ by which the believers are called.

2.5.1.en: May you look to God who stands before you, so that you declare the truth and show partiality to no one out of fear of his position or authority, or for any benefit you hope for from him, and honor everyone, however weak or poor they may be.

2.6.0.en: The royal law: that is, the law of Christ, the heavenly King, and it is love.

2.6.1.en: The law of Christ, that is, His rule, is love, and this moves us to love all around us, in application of the commandment “Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself” (Lev 19:18), so the Apostle blesses the conduct of love toward all.

2.7.0.en: Partiality is against love, for it is a transgression of the rule of Christianity and is counted a great sin.

2.8.0.en: Do not justify yourselves by keeping many commandments and acts of worship in the Church while transgressing the most important thing, which is love, the spirit of the law of Christ, for by this you are guilty toward Christ and all His commandments.

2.9.0.en: Persisting in one sin deserves death. It is not right to persist in a sin such as murder while being careful about adultery, for the Law of Moses sentences the murderer to death because he broke this commandment, despite his care for the rest of the law.

2.10.0.en: The law of liberty: the rule of Christ, that is, love.

2.10.1.en: So in the New Testament we must hold fast to all His commandments and not persist in neglecting one of them by persisting in partiality, for this deserves destruction.

2.11.0.en: Mercy rejoiceth against judgment: just judgment is to give everyone who has a right his right, but mercy in Christianity gives more than the right that people deserve, as long as they are in need. Whoever does not show mercy to others, so that he shows partiality to the rich and despises the poor, God will not have mercy on him and will sentence him to eternal destruction; rather, the rule of Christianity is mercy, especially since God showed us His mercy in redemption and in forgiving our sins every day, which moves us to have compassion on all and to show them mercy.

2.11.1.en: God allowed some to suffer poverty or sickness or any need, so that the love and mercy of others toward them might appear, and all might hold together as members of one body and rejoice in the love that binds them and forget their pains; so do not neglect any needy person around you.

2.12.0.en: The Apostle James found the poor dying of hunger and the rich not moving, so he spoke of the uselessness of faith without works.

2.12.1.en: This does not contradict the Apostle Paul, who says, “Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law” (Rom 3:28), because Paul is speaking of the works of the Law that are not necessary for salvation, and for that reason he spoke of the necessity of faith that works by love and spoke of striving, service and giving. This agrees with the Apostle James, who here speaks of the works that are the fruit of living faith.

2.12.2.en: In the following verses the Apostle offers practical examples of the necessity of joining good works to faith as a condition for the believer’s salvation.

2.13.0.en: The first example: the Apostle gives an example. If you have a brother or sister who is poor and you show kindness to them in words without offering a positive deed, you are not meeting their needs.

2.14.0.en: The second example: faith without works is like a dead body that has no spirit; the spirit is the works, which show that faith is alive. Faith that has no works is theoretical faith, dead in itself, and it leads you to death.

2.15.0.en: The third example shows the importance of good works in a dialogue that takes place between a person who has faith without works and a second who has good works resulting from his faith. The second says to the first: if your faith is real, show it to me, because it cannot be shown without works, but I by my good works show you that my faith is real.

2.16.0.en: The fourth example also confirms the uselessness of faith without works. If a person has faith in the one God but has no good works, this profits him nothing but condemns him on the last day, because his faith did not bear good works. It is like the demons, who believe that God is one and recognize this so greatly that they reach the point of great fear of God, which is expressed by trembling, yet they continue in their evils, so this theoretical faith of theirs, not accompanied by good works, condemns them on the last day.

2.17.0.en: In the true believer the works of love appear in his life, but the “vain man”, that is, the one who has faith without good works, his faith is vain. And the Apostle goes on to prove to him by other evidences that his faith, void of works, is dead.

2.18.1.en: The Apostle James uses an example, Abraham, the father of the Jewish people, whose working faith appeared when he offered Isaac his son as a sacrifice, believing that God was able to raise him from the dead (Rom 4:3). Thus the work shared with Abraham’s faith, and by his work his faith was made perfect, that is, by his offering Isaac as a sacrifice he perfected his faith in God, who is able to raise from the dead.

2.19.1.en: By works, that is, by Abraham’s offering Isaac his son as a sacrifice, the saying of the Holy Bible in (Gen 15:6) was fulfilled, so he perfected his faith, by which he became righteous before God, and even rose to the degree of friendship with God. And this is the fifth proof that justification takes place by faith and works and not by faith alone.

2.20.1.en: The Apostle gives an example of the joining of works to faith among the Gentiles who believed, and not only the Jews. Rahab, the Gentile harlot, believed in the power of the God of Israel and hid the two men whom Joshua had sent to spy out the Promised Land, so that they would not be killed (Josh 2:1-6), and she hung a scarlet cord on her house, a sign of faith in the blood of Christ the Redeemer, so God rescued her from destruction with the idolaters, the inhabitants of Jericho, for her faith that worked by love. By this Rahab declared that works are like the spirit in the body and give it life; if there are no works, faith, which is like the body, will become dead.

2.20.2.en: Do not be content with appreciating the troubles and needs of others, but join your feelings with works of love that you offer them, even small works, as much as you can, knowing that your work, however small, has value before God, for the cup of cold water will not lose its reward.
